questions.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-4y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-4(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-4\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=4 \\ {a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-4)=\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {a}_{n}=\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+16)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+16)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

questions.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-2y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)-2(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))=2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-2\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)=2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=2 \\ {a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-2)=\frac{4(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {a}_{n}=\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+2)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{4{\pi }^{2}}=2\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=2\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x))+x(-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)-4{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x):$

$$
[-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)-4{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+4{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\pi A=0 \\ 4\pi B=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{16\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{x}{16\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A=1 \\ 2\pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{8}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{8}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{8}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})=\frac{8}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=\frac{8}{9} \\ 3\pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{8}{27\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=-\frac{8x}{27\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$
